hook: The astronomer who found the laws that move the planets.

pages.x: Johannes Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt, in Germany. Smallpox left him with weak eyes and crippled hands. At six his mother took him up a hill to see the Great Comet of 1577. He trained to be a Lutheran minister, but was sent to teach mathematics in Graz.

In 1595 he thought he had found God's plan: the orbits of the six known planets fitted around the five perfect solids, the cube, the pyramid and the rest, nested one inside another. It was wrong, but it got him noticed.

In 1600 he went to Prague to work for Tycho Brahe, the greatest sky-watcher of the age, who wore a metal nose after losing his own in a duel. When Tycho died in 1601, Kepler inherited his priceless records, and his job as imperial mathematician.
After years of sums on the orbit of Mars, he found that planets move not in circles but in ellipses, with the Sun off-centre, and go faster when they are nearer the Sun.
pages.fx: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion let Newton work out the law of gravity, and they still guide spacecraft today.

pages.x: He wrote Somnium, "The Dream", about a boy carried to the Moon by spirits, describing how the Earth would look from there. It is often called the first work of science fiction.

In 1615 his elderly mother, Katharina, was accused of witchcraft by a neighbour. Kepler spent years defending her, and in 1621 won her freedom, after she had been chained in a cell for over a year and shown the instruments of torture.

Kepler discovered the laws by which planets move, turning astronomy from geometry into physics. NASA's Kepler space telescope, which found thousands of planets around other stars, was named after him.
pts: Discovered the three laws of planetary motion
Prepared the way for Newton's gravity
